name: Wade Robichaux
languages: Louisiana French (badly, and only the swearing is fluent)
equipment: Leather jacket, Navy deck jacket, the stencil scrubbed off the back
Brass knuckles, in the left jacket pocket, worn smooth
.45 automatic (Navy-issue Colt, which he should have turned in and did not), 7 rounds loaded, in his waistband at the back
A good suit, a size too small in the shoulders, for funerals and job interviews, of which there have been more of the first
A rigger's marlinspike and a coil of rope, from habit
Cigarette case with a dent in it from a Japanese bullet, he says, and from a bar door, he means
His discharge papers and the honourable discharge pin, the "ruptured duck"
A pawn ticket for his Navy boxing trophy, $6
features: Seen Worse (Ex-Service origin: advantage on saves against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his reaction and any readied action)

Hard Knocks (Heavy: unarmed strikes deal 1d6 + STR; once per turn, +1d4 bludgeoning when he hits with a fist or a bludgeoning Melee weapon; a creature he drops to 0 with one is knocked out unless he chooses otherwise; he can deliver a knockout blow with fists or any of these weapons)
Thick Skull (Heavy: advantage on CON saves against knockout blows and stunning; once per long rest, when dropped to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 instead)

The Look (Heavy, 2nd level: as an action, one creature within 30 ft that can see him makes a WIS save, DC 13, or is frightened until the end of his next turn; outside combat it replaces an Intimidation check, and on a failure the target answers one question truthfully or does one reasonable thing he tells it)
Style: Enforcer (Heavy, 3rd level: when he hits with a melee attack, he can push the target 10 ft or knock it prone if it fails a STR save, DC 13)

Fight Crowd (Prizefighter background: managers, trainers, promoters and gamblers know him; he can get a seat at any fight in town, find out who is fixing what, and name the bookmaker who takes the big bets)

personality.traits: I stand too close to people without meaning to. I laugh loudly, eat fast and say thank you to waitresses. I am slower with words than I am with my hands, and I know it, and I hate being hurried.
personality.ideals: A man who works ought to get paid for it. I never thought hard about which men that meant until this week.
personality.bonds: My mother on Dauphine Street in the Bywater, who had an operation in January that I paid for with money I borrowed from the wrong man. The Ste. Claire yard, where I learned my trade and where I would go back tomorrow if they would have me.
personality.flaws: I owe Emile Gravier three hundred dollars, and he knows where my mother lives. And in 1941, on the yard, I watched the Black welders do the work and the white men take the rate, and I said nothing, because it was the custom, and because I was one of the white men.

appearance: A broad, thick-necked man of thirty-one with a fighter's face: flattened nose, a cauliflower left ear, scar tissue over both eyes, and surprisingly gentle grey eyes in the middle of it. Red-brown hair, big scarred hands, a Navy deck jacket and a cap. He looks like trouble and he is mostly polite.
backstory: Wade Robichaux grew up in the Bywater three blocks from the Industrial Canal, where the ship horns woke him as a child, and at seventeen he went to work at Ste. Claire Marine Ways as a rigger's helper, hauling steel plate into place with chain falls for the welders. He was good at it, and he was a better boxer: he fought as a light-heavyweight in the Coliseum Arena on Saturday nights and won more than he lost. In 1942 he joined the Navy, fought for his ship's team across the Pacific, and spent the last year of the war on a repair ship at Ulithi, rigging patches onto torpedoed hulls. He came home in December 1945 to find the yard laying off two thousand men, his old foreman dead, and his mother sick. Ste. Claire would not rehire him. Emile Gravier, the stevedore contractor who supplies the yard with labour, lent him three hundred dollars for his mother's operation at an interest rate that doubles every month, and has since offered to forget the whole debt if Wade will do 'a little work' on the docks, which means breaking arms. On Friday morning Wade is at the shape-up at the foot of Poland Avenue when the word comes along the wharf that they have pulled Marcel Fontenot, the pay clerk, out of the canal, and that the police say he was drunk. Wade knew Marcel. Everybody at Ste. Claire knew Marcel, because Marcel filled the pay envelopes. And Marcel Fontenot never took a drink in his life.
